topics.title: Java fundamentals
topics.summary: Foundational questions about what Java is, how it runs, and why it remains dominant in backend systems.

questions.question: What is Java and why is it used so much for backend development?
answer: Java source code is compiled into bytecode and executed by the Java Virtual Machine. That gives teams a stable runtime model, strong tooling, and the ability to run the same application on different operating systems with minimal change.

For backend development, Java is popular because it combines type safety, predictable performance, mature concurrency support, excellent observability tooling, and a huge ecosystem around Spring Boot, build tools, database access, testing, messaging, and cloud deployment.

In interviews, a strong answer should not stop at "Java is platform independent". Connect Java to real backend concerns: maintainability, hiring, long-term support, transaction-heavy systems, monitoring, production debugging, and safe refactoring in large codebases.

The trade-off is that Java can feel verbose and requires discipline around architecture. Good Java backend code is not just code that compiles; it has clear boundaries, testable services, useful errors, and observable runtime behavior.
questions.answerShort: Java is a strongly typed, object-oriented language that runs on the JVM, which makes it portable, mature, and practical for long-lived backend systems.
applyOrPitfalls: Apply this knowledge when explaining why Java is chosen for APIs, internal platforms, banking systems, enterprise workflows, data-heavy services, and Spring Boot applications.
Do not answer only with "write once, run anywhere". That is true but too shallow for real interviews; explain what the JVM and ecosystem give backend teams in production.
Do not blame Java or the JVM before measuring. Performance problems often come from database access, bad object allocation patterns, missing indexes, chatty APIs, or poor transaction boundaries.
When reviewing Java code, look for clear domain names, small services, explicit dependencies, focused tests, and logs that help operate the system.
explanation: The JVM is the important bridge: Java code becomes bytecode, and the JVM handles class loading, memory management, JIT compilation, garbage collection, and runtime execution.

Backend teams like Java because large applications need more than syntax. They need stable libraries, predictable deployment, good profiling tools, transaction support, mature security libraries, and conventions that many developers already understand.

A practical interview answer should mention both strengths and trade-offs. Java is strong for enterprise backend systems, but poor design can still create slow, tightly coupled, hard-to-test applications.
practice: Explain Java in two versions: a beginner version in three sentences, then an interview version that includes JVM, ecosystem, maintainability, and production operations.
Create a tiny Java class, compile it with `javac`, run it with `java`, and explain what happens between source code and runtime.
Look at a Spring Boot controller-service-repository flow and identify which parts are Java language fundamentals and which parts are framework behavior.

questions.question: Differentiate JDK, JRE, and JVM.
answer: JVM means Java Virtual Machine. It loads bytecode, verifies it, executes it, manages memory, performs garbage collection, and may JIT-compile hot code into machine code.
JRE means Java Runtime Environment. It contains the JVM plus runtime libraries needed to run Java applications, but it is not the full developer toolkit.

JDK means Java Development Kit. It includes the runtime plus tools used by developers: `javac` to compile, `java` to run, `jar` to package, `javadoc` to generate documentation, and debugging/diagnostic tools.
Interview framing: if you only need to run an application, you need a runtime. If you need to compile, package, debug, or build Java code, you need the JDK.

In production, this topic often appears through startup errors, dependency mismatch, memory pressure, warm-up behavior, container image choices, and confusing differences between local and deployed environments.
For learning, separate the source-code idea from the runtime behavior: what is checked by the compiler, what is loaded by the JVM, and what can still fail only when the application runs.
questions.answerShort: JVM runs bytecode, JRE provides the runtime needed to run Java apps, and JDK adds developer tools such as javac, jar, jshell, and javadoc.
applyOrPitfalls: Apply this when a machine can run Java but cannot compile because `javac` is missing.
Apply this when choosing a Docker base image: a full JDK image is useful for builds, while a smaller runtime image is better for production when possible.
Do not say "JDK contains JVM only". The JDK is a full development toolkit, not just the virtual machine.
Do not debug classpath, compiler, and runtime errors as if they were the same category. Separate build-time and runtime concerns first.
explanation: A simple mental model is: JDK is for building, JRE is for running, JVM is the engine that executes bytecode.
Modern JDK distributions often bundle what you need to both build and run, so learners may not see a separate JRE installation anymore. The conceptual distinction is still important.
This distinction matters when debugging CI/CD, Docker images, local setup, IDE configuration, and production runtime images.
practice: Run `java -version` and `javac -version`, then explain what each command proves about your environment.
Compile a small class with `javac`, run it with `java`, then package it with `jar` to understand the development flow.
Explain to a teammate why a production container may not need every tool that exists in a developer JDK.

questions.question: What steps does Java source code go through before it runs?
answer: The flow starts with a `.java` source file. `javac` compiles it into `.class` bytecode, which is a platform-neutral instruction format for the JVM.
At runtime, class loaders locate and load classes. The JVM verifies bytecode for safety, links classes, initializes static state, and prepares the code for execution.
The JVM may interpret bytecode at first. When a method becomes hot, the JIT compiler can compile optimized machine code for the current CPU.
For backend work, this flow matters because class loading, dependency versions, startup time, warm-up, JIT behavior, and memory allocation can all affect production behavior.
practice: Create a small class, compile it with `javac`, inspect it with `javap -c`, then explain the bytecode at a high level.
Deliberately rename a class file or remove it from the classpath and observe the kind of runtime error you get.
Explain the difference between a syntax error, a class-loading error, and an exception thrown after the program starts.
questions.answerShort: Java source code is compiled to bytecode, loaded by the JVM, verified, interpreted or JIT-compiled, and then executed while the JVM manages memory and runtime services.
applyOrPitfalls: Apply this when diagnosing build-vs-runtime differences, classpath problems, dependency conflicts, and container startup issues.
Do not assume the code you wrote is exactly what the CPU executes. The compiler, bytecode, class loader, and JIT all participate in the runtime path.
Do not benchmark a Java method once and treat the result as final. Warm-up and JIT optimization matter.
When debugging, separate compile-time errors, class-loading errors, runtime exceptions, and performance behavior.
explanation: The source file is not what the JVM directly runs. The JVM runs bytecode, and bytecode is what gives Java its portability.
JIT compilation explains why Java performance can improve after warm-up. This is also why naive benchmarks can be misleading.
Understanding this flow helps when debugging `ClassNotFoundException`, `NoSuchMethodError`, dependency conflicts, slow startup, and strange behavior between local and production environments.

questions.question: Is Java completely object-oriented?
answer: Java is not a pure object-oriented language because primitive values such as `int`, `long`, `double`, `boolean`, and `char` are not objects. They are stored and operated on differently from normal object references.

At the same time, Java strongly supports object-oriented design through classes, interfaces, encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, packages, and access control. Most backend application code is designed around objects and contracts.
The practical answer is: Java is object-oriented enough for real application design, but it intentionally keeps primitives because they are efficient and useful for low-level value operations.
In interviews, mention autoboxing and wrapper types such as `Integer` and `Long` because they bridge primitives with APIs that require objects, especially generics and collections.
questions.answerShort: Java is not a pure object-oriented language because primitive values such as `int`, `long`, `double`, `boolean`, and `char` are not objects. They are stored and operated on differently from normal object references.
applyOrPitfalls: Apply this when explaining primitive vs wrapper behavior, autoboxing, null-pointer risk, collection usage, and performance-sensitive code.
Do not say Java is completely object-oriented. That answer ignores primitives and usually sounds memorized.
Be careful when unboxing wrapper values. `Integer count = null; int value = count;` throws `NullPointerException`.
Use primitives for simple non-null numeric state, and wrappers when you need nullability, generics, or framework binding.
explanation: Pure object-oriented languages model everything as an object. Java does not do that because primitives are special language-level values.
This trade-off improves performance and memory usage, but it creates important details around autoboxing, null handling, equality, generics, and collections.
A strong answer connects the definition to real code: `List<int>` is invalid, but `List<Integer>` works because generics require reference types.

questions.question: Why is Java cross-platform?
answer: Java source code is compiled into JVM bytecode instead of native machine code for one operating system. That bytecode is stored in `.class` files or packaged into `.jar` files.
A compatible JVM exists for different operating systems and CPU architectures. The JVM translates and executes the same bytecode for the current platform.
This is the meaning of "write once, run anywhere" in practical terms: the same compiled artifact can often run across environments if the correct JVM and dependencies are available.
In backend work, cross-platform support helps with developer machines, CI environments, containers, Linux servers, and cloud deployment.
questions.answerShort: Java is cross-platform because `javac` produces bytecode, and any compatible JVM can execute that bytecode on its operating system.
applyOrPitfalls: Apply this when packaging Java applications as JARs, Docker images, or deployable services across different environments.
Do not claim Java code is automatically environment-independent. File paths, timezone, locale, charset, native libraries, and OS permissions can still break behavior.
When a program works locally but fails on Linux, check environment differences before blaming the language.
Prefer configuration and platform-neutral APIs over hard-coded machine-specific assumptions.
explanation: The portability comes from the JVM layer, not from magic in the source code. The JVM is platform-specific; the bytecode is portable.
Real portability still depends on avoiding OS-specific file paths, encodings, native libraries, and environment assumptions.
For interviews, mention both the bytecode/JVM mechanism and the real-world caveat that dependencies and environment configuration still matter.
practice: Compile a class on your machine and run the generated `.class` file from another directory with the correct classpath.
Write code that uses `Path.of(...)` instead of hard-coded Windows or Linux path separators.
Explain why the JVM is platform-specific but Java bytecode is portable.

questions.question: How is Java different from JavaScript even though the names look similar?
answer: Java is a statically typed language compiled to JVM bytecode. It is widely used for backend services, enterprise systems, Android legacy code, batch jobs, and large systems that need strong tooling and maintainability.

JavaScript is dynamically typed by default and originally ran in browsers. With Node.js it is also used on the backend, especially for web APIs, tooling, real-time applications, and full-stack JavaScript teams.

The names are historically confusing, but the languages are not close relatives. They differ in runtime, type model, package ecosystem, concurrency model, deployment style, and typical architecture choices.
For "How is Java different from JavaScript even though the names look similar?", start with the main rule and immediately connect it to a concrete code path.
In Java fundamentals, the answer should name which behavior changes and why that change matters.
questions.answerShort: Java and JavaScript are different languages with different runtimes, type systems, ecosystems, concurrency models, and common backend use cases.
applyOrPitfalls: Apply this when choosing a stack, comparing backend platforms, or explaining why a team might choose Spring Boot, Node.js, or another runtime.
Do not say JavaScript is a simplified Java. That is wrong and signals shallow understanding.
Do not choose a language only by popularity. Consider ecosystem fit, operational maturity, developer experience, hiring, and existing system constraints.
When moving between Java and JavaScript, pay attention to type behavior, equality rules, async behavior, package management, and runtime error patterns.
explanation: Java usually catches many type errors at compile time; JavaScript often catches them at runtime unless TypeScript or tooling is used.
Java backend concurrency commonly uses threads, executors, virtual threads, and framework-managed request handling. JavaScript commonly uses an event loop and asynchronous I/O.
The important skill is not memorizing differences but understanding how those differences affect debugging, testing, scaling, and team workflow.
